notes.definition: The eye is a sense organ containing receptors sensitive to light intensity and colour. Its structures refract light to focus an image on the retina, and accommodation changes the shape of the lens to focus on near or distant objects.
explanation: Light enters the eye through the cornea, a transparent layer at the front that refracts (bends) light. The iris is the coloured ring of muscle that controls the size of the pupil, the gap in its centre, and so controls how much light reaches the retina. In bright light the pupil becomes smaller to protect the retina; in dim light it becomes larger to let more light in.

The lens refracts light further to focus it on the retina at the back of the eye. The retina contains receptor cells sensitive to light intensity and colour. When stimulated, they send electrical impulses along the optic nerve to the brain. The sclera is the tough white outer layer that protects the eye and keeps its shape.

The lens is held in place by suspensory ligaments, which connect it to a ring of ciliary muscles. Accommodation is the process of changing the shape of the lens to focus on near or distant objects. To focus on a near object, the ciliary muscles contract, the suspensory ligaments loosen, and the lens becomes thicker, so it refracts light rays strongly.

To focus on a distant object, the ciliary muscles relax, the suspensory ligaments are pulled tight, and the lens is pulled thin, so it only slightly refracts light rays. Light from distant objects arrives almost parallel and needs less refraction than the spreading rays from a near object.

Myopia (short-sightedness) and hyperopia (long-sightedness) are common defects in which light rays do not focus on the retina. In myopia, distant objects look blurred because light is focused in front of the retina (the lens is too curved or the eyeball too long). It is corrected with a concave (diverging) lens. In hyperopia, near objects look blurred because light would be focused behind the retina (the lens is too flat or the eyeball too short). It is corrected with a convex (converging) lens.

Spectacle lenses are the usual treatment, but new technologies include hard and soft contact lenses that sit on the cornea, laser surgery to change the shape of the cornea, and replacing the lens of the eye with an artificial one. Each has benefits and risks: contact lenses can cause infections if not cleaned, and surgery carries a risk of damage to the eye.
keyFacts: The retina contains receptors sensitive to light intensity and colour.
The optic nerve carries impulses from the retina to the brain.
The sclera is the tough white outer layer that protects the eye.
The cornea is transparent and refracts light into the eye.
The iris controls the size of the pupil and so how much light reaches the retina.
Ciliary muscles and suspensory ligaments change the shape of the lens.
Near object: ciliary muscles contract, ligaments loosen, lens thicker, refracts strongly.
Distant object: ciliary muscles relax, ligaments tight, lens thin, refracts slightly.
Myopia: focus in front of retina, corrected by a concave lens.
Hyperopia: focus behind retina, corrected by a convex lens.
New treatments: hard and soft contact lenses, laser surgery on the cornea, replacement lens.

keyTerms.definition: The light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye containing receptor cells sensitive to light intensity and colour.
The bundle of sensory neurones that carries impulses from the retina to the brain.
The tough, white outer layer of the eye that protects it.
The transparent front part of the eye that refracts light as it enters.
The coloured ring of muscle that controls the size of the pupil and the amount of light reaching the retina.
A ring of muscle that contracts or relaxes to change the shape of the lens.
Fibres that connect the lens to the ciliary muscles and hold it in place.
The process of changing the shape of the lens to focus on near or distant objects.
Short-sightedness: distant objects are blurred because light focuses in front of the retina.
Long-sightedness: near objects are blurred because light would focus behind the retina.

workedExamples.title: Describing accommodation
workedExamples.question: A student looks up from reading a book to watch a bird far away. Describe the changes in the eye that allow the bird to be seen clearly.
steps: Identify the change: from a near object to a distant object.
The lens is pulled thin, so it refracts light only slightly and the image is focused on the retina.
workedExamples.answer: Ciliary muscles relax, suspensory ligaments tighten, lens becomes thinner and refracts light less, so light from the distant bird is focused on the retina.

workedExamples.title: Interpreting a ray diagram
workedExamples.question: A ray diagram shows parallel light rays from a distant object meeting at a point in front of a person's retina. Name the defect and describe how it is corrected.
steps: Rays meet in front of the retina, so they are refracted too much.
A concave (diverging) lens spreads the rays out before they enter the eye.
The eye then focuses the rays further back, on the retina.
workedExamples.answer: Myopia. Correct it with a concave lens (or contact lenses, or laser surgery to reshape the cornea) so rays focus on the retina.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the ciliary muscles contract to make the lens thin.
misconceptions.right: In fact contracting ciliary muscles loosen the suspensory ligaments, so the lens becomes thicker (for near objects). Relaxed ciliary muscles let the ligaments pull the lens thin.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the lens does all of the refraction.
misconceptions.right: In fact the cornea also refracts light, and does most of it. The lens fine-tunes the focus.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often mix up myopia and hyperopia.
misconceptions.right: Myopia is short-sightedness (near objects are clear, distant ones blurred). Hyperopia is long-sightedness (distant objects clear, near ones blurred).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the pupil is a structure that contracts.
misconceptions.right: In fact the pupil is just a gap; the iris muscles change its size.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a concave lens corrects long-sightedness.
misconceptions.right: In fact a concave (diverging) lens corrects myopia; a convex (converging) lens corrects hyperopia.

realWorld: Opticians use eye tests and lenses of different strength to prescribe spectacles or contact lenses for myopia and hyperopia.
Laser eye surgery reshapes the cornea to correct vision, so many people no longer need glasses.
Cataract surgery replaces a cloudy lens with an artificial lens and is one of the most common operations in the UK.
As people age the lens becomes less elastic, which is why many older adults need reading glasses.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is in separate Biology (8461) only, not in Combined Science Trilogy.
Relate the retina, optic nerve, sclera, cornea, iris, ciliary muscles and suspensory ligaments to their functions.
Accommodation, myopia and hyperopia, ray diagrams and their correction with lenses and new technologies.
examTips: For accommodation, always give the three linked steps in order: ciliary muscles, suspensory ligaments, lens shape, then say how much the lens refracts light.
Use the word "refract", not "reflect", when describing what the cornea and lens do to light.
Remember: Myopia → Minus (concave) lens. Hyperopia → convex lens.
On ray diagrams, check where the rays meet: in front of the retina means myopia, behind it means hyperopia.
If asked to evaluate a treatment, give a benefit, a risk and a conclusion.
summary: The eye contains receptors in the retina sensitive to light intensity and colour.
Cornea and lens refract light to focus it on the retina; the optic nerve carries impulses to the brain.
The iris controls pupil size; the sclera protects the eye.
Accommodation: near object, lens thick; distant object, lens thin.
Myopia is corrected with a concave lens, hyperopia with a convex lens.
New treatments: contact lenses, laser surgery on the cornea, replacement lenses.

Connect the lens to the ciliary muscles and hold it in place.
Changing the shape of the lens to focus on near or distant objects.

flashcards.front: Eye focusing on a near object?
flashcards.back: Ciliary muscles contract, suspensory ligaments loosen, lens thicker, refracts light strongly.

flashcards.front: Eye focusing on a distant object?
flashcards.back: Ciliary muscles relax, suspensory ligaments pulled tight, lens thin, refracts light slightly.

flashcards.front: What is myopia and how is it corrected?
flashcards.back: Short-sightedness: light focuses in front of the retina. Corrected by a concave lens.

flashcards.front: What is hyperopia and how is it corrected?
flashcards.back: Long-sightedness: light would focus behind the retina. Corrected by a convex lens.

flashcards.back: Hard and soft contact lenses, laser surgery to reshape the cornea, replacement lens.

questions.question: Which part of the eye contains receptor cells that are sensitive to light?
markScheme: 1 mark: retina
questions.explanation: The retina contains receptors sensitive to light intensity and colour. The cornea refracts light, the sclera protects and the iris controls pupil size.

questions.question: What is the function of the optic nerve?
options: To carry impulses from the retina to the brain
To change the shape of the lens
To control the size of the pupil
To refract light onto the retina
markScheme: 1 mark: carries impulses from retina to brain
questions.explanation: The optic nerve is made of sensory neurones that carry impulses from the retina to the brain.

questions.question: Which part of the eye is the tough, white outer layer?
markScheme: 1 mark: sclera
questions.explanation: The sclera is the tough white outer layer that protects the eye. The cornea is the transparent part at the front.

questions.question: Which part of the eye is transparent and refracts light as it enters?
markScheme: 1 mark: cornea
questions.explanation: The cornea is transparent so light can pass through, and its curved shape refracts light.

questions.question: Which part of the eye controls how much light reaches the retina?
markScheme: 1 mark: iris
questions.explanation: The iris is a ring of muscle that changes the size of the pupil, so it controls how much light enters and reaches the retina.

questions.question: What happens in the eye when a person focuses on a near object?
options: Ciliary muscles contract, suspensory ligaments loosen, lens becomes thicker
Ciliary muscles relax, suspensory ligaments tighten, lens becomes thinner
Ciliary muscles contract, suspensory ligaments tighten, lens becomes thinner
Ciliary muscles relax, suspensory ligaments loosen, lens becomes thicker
markScheme: 1 mark: ciliary muscles contract, ligaments loosen, lens thicker
questions.explanation: For near objects the lens must refract light strongly, so it must be thicker. Contracting ciliary muscles reduce the tension on the suspensory ligaments, letting the lens become fatter.

questions.question: What is accommodation?
options: Changing the size of the pupil in bright light
Replacing a damaged lens with an artificial one
Changing the shape of the lens to focus on near or distant objects
Sending impulses from the retina to the brain
markScheme: 1 mark: changing the shape of the lens to focus
questions.explanation: Accommodation is the process of changing the shape of the lens to focus on near or distant objects. Changing pupil size is controlled by the iris.

questions.question: In a person with myopia, where are light rays from a distant object focused?
markScheme: 1 mark: in front of the retina
questions.explanation: In myopia (short-sightedness) light is refracted too much, so rays from distant objects meet in front of the retina and the image is blurred.

questions.question: Which type of spectacle lens is used to correct hyperopia?
markScheme: 1 mark: convex (converging) lens
questions.explanation: In hyperopia light would focus behind the retina, so a convex lens is used to refract the rays inwards before they enter the eye.

questions.question: As people age, their lens becomes less elastic and cannot become thicker. Which problem is this most likely to cause?
markScheme: 1 mark: difficulty focusing on near objects
questions.explanation: Near objects need a thick lens that refracts light strongly. If the lens cannot become thick, light from near objects is focused behind the retina, which is why older people often need reading glasses.

questions.question: How does laser eye surgery correct vision?
options: It changes the shape of the cornea
markScheme: 1 mark: changes the shape of the cornea
questions.explanation: Laser surgery reshapes the cornea so that it refracts light by the correct amount and rays focus on the retina.

questions.question: A person's eyeball is longer than normal from front to back. Which statement explains their vision problem?
options: Light focuses behind the retina, so they have hyperopia
Light focuses in front of the retina, so they have myopia
Light cannot pass through the cornea, so they cannot see
The lens cannot change shape, so they cannot accommodate
markScheme: 1 mark: light focuses in front of the retina, so myopia
questions.explanation: With a longer eyeball the retina is further back, so the point where rays meet is in front of the retina. Distant objects look blurred: myopia.

questions.question: The receptor cells in the retina are sensitive to which two things?
markScheme: 1 mark: light intensity and colour
questions.explanation: The eye is a sense organ containing receptors sensitive to light intensity and colour.

questions.question: Which two parts of the eye refract light to focus it on the retina?
markScheme: 1 mark: cornea and lens
questions.explanation: The cornea and lens are both transparent and curved, so they refract light. The iris controls light entry but does not refract it.

questions.question: State the function of the iris and explain why this is important in bright light.
markScheme: 1 mark: controls the size of the pupil / amount of light entering
1 mark: makes pupil smaller in bright light to protect the retina from damage
questions.explanation: The iris adjusts the size of the pupil. In bright light the pupil is made smaller so that less light reaches the retina, preventing damage.

questions.question: State the function of the suspensory ligaments.
markScheme: 1 mark: connect the lens to the ciliary muscles / hold the lens in place
questions.explanation: Suspensory ligaments hold the lens and transmit the pull from the ciliary muscles to change its shape.

questions.question: Describe how the eye changes to focus on a distant object.
markScheme: 1 mark: ciliary muscles relax
1 mark: suspensory ligaments are pulled tight
1 mark: lens is pulled thin, so it refracts light only slightly
questions.explanation: For distant objects light arrives nearly parallel and needs little refraction, so the lens is pulled thin.

questions.question: Explain how a concave lens corrects myopia.
markScheme: 1 mark: concave lens spreads out / diverges the light rays before they enter the eye
1 mark: so the rays are focused further back, on the retina
questions.explanation: In myopia rays focus in front of the retina. A diverging lens spreads them out so the eye's focus moves back onto the retina.

questions.question: Other than spectacles, name two technologies that can be used to correct myopia or hyperopia.
markScheme: 1 mark each, max 2: hard contact lenses; soft contact lenses; laser surgery to change the shape of the cornea; replacement lens
questions.explanation: AQA names hard and soft contact lenses, laser surgery to change the shape of the cornea and replacement lenses.

questions.question: Explain why the lens must be thicker to focus light from a near object than from a distant object.
markScheme: 1 mark: light rays from a near object are spreading out / diverging more
1 mark: so they need to be refracted more strongly (by a thicker lens) to focus on the retina
questions.explanation: Rays from a distant object are almost parallel. Rays from a near object spread out, so a more strongly refracting (thicker) lens is needed to bring them to a focus on the retina.

questions.question: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of laser eye surgery compared with wearing spectacles.
markScheme: 1 mark: advantage: permanent / no need to wear or buy glasses / no lenses to lose or break
1 mark: disadvantage: risk of damage to the eye / infection / cannot be reversed / expensive
questions.explanation: Surgery removes the need for glasses, but like any surgery it carries risks and cannot easily be undone.

questions.question: Give one advantage and one risk of wearing contact lenses rather than spectacles.
markScheme: 1 mark: advantage: not easily seen / do not get knocked off or steam up / good for sport
1 mark: risk: eye infection if not cleaned / irritation or damage to the cornea
questions.explanation: Contact lenses sit on the cornea, so they are convenient but need careful hygiene.

questions.question: A person walks from a dark room into bright sunlight. Describe and explain what happens to their pupils.
markScheme: 1 mark: the pupils become smaller
1 mark: muscles in the iris change the pupil size (automatically, by a reflex)
1 mark: less light reaches the retina, so the retina is not damaged
questions.explanation: This automatic response protects the light-sensitive receptor cells in the retina from damage by very bright light.

questions.question: Some artificial replacement lenses cannot change shape. Suggest why a person with this type of replacement lens may need glasses for reading.
markScheme: 1 mark: the lens cannot become thicker / cannot accommodate
1 mark: so light from near objects (such as a book) is not refracted enough to focus on the retina / focuses behind the retina
questions.explanation: Reading requires accommodation for a near object. A rigid lens is usually set for distant vision, so a convex reading lens provides the extra refraction.

questions.question: In a person's eye, light from a near object is brought to a focus behind the retina. Name this defect and the type of lens used to correct it.
markScheme: 1 mark: hyperopia / long-sightedness
1 mark: convex / converging lens
questions.explanation: Focus behind the retina means the light is not refracted enough, which is hyperopia. A convex lens adds extra refraction.

questions.question: State the function of the cornea.
markScheme: 1 mark: refracts light (as it enters the eye) / transparent to let light in
questions.explanation: The cornea is transparent and curved, so it lets light in and refracts it.

questions.question: Describe how the eye focuses light from a near object onto the retina.
markScheme: Indicative content: light enters through the cornea, which refracts light; passes through the pupil; ciliary muscles contract; suspensory ligaments loosen / slacken; lens becomes thicker / more rounded; lens refracts light more strongly; light is focused on the retina; receptors in the retina are stimulated and impulses travel along the optic nerve to the brain.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): the correct sequence of ciliary muscles, suspensory ligaments and lens shape changes, linked to stronger refraction and focusing on the retina.

questions.question: Compare myopia and hyperopia. In your answer, describe what happens to light rays in each defect and how each can be corrected.
markScheme: Indicative content: both are common defects where light rays do not focus on the retina; myopia is short-sightedness: distant objects blurred, near objects clear; rays focus in front of the retina; caused by lens too curved / refracting too much or eyeball too long; corrected with a concave (diverging) lens that spreads rays out; hyperopia is long-sightedness: near objects blurred, distant objects clear; rays would focus behind the retina; caused by lens too flat / not refracting enough or eyeball too short; corrected with a convex (converging) lens that refracts rays inwards; both can also be treated with hard or soft contact lenses, laser surgery to change the shape of the cornea, or a replacement lens; evaluation of treatments, for example surgery is permanent but has risks.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a clear comparison of both defects, with correct ray paths, causes and correct lens types explained, plus other technologies.
